1.pericope_label: When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt. And it shall be, when ye are come nigh unto the battle, that the priest shall approach and speak unto the people, And shall say unto them, Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them; For the Lord your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.

schools.summary: Read the whole chapter as governing wars against nations outside Canaan and state its purpose as one humane principle, that the people of God were to spare as far as possible the lives of their own soldiers and of their enemies alike, which is what the exemptions, the offer of peace, the sparing of women and children and the protection of the fruit-trees all serve; take the opening phrase as general rather than confined to the immediate conquest, since Moses foresees a gradual completion; and identify the speaker precisely as the priest who accompanied the army, not the high priest, whom the Rabbins style the anointed of the battle on the strength of a single passage.

File the law under the first commandment rather than the civil code, since its point is that Israel should wage war under the auspices of God and rest its hope of safety on nothing but the invocation of his name; draw from that the general rule that the worship of God is by no means to be passed over in civil and earthly government, for though such government aims directly at equity between men, religion always ought to hold the first place; and count the four expressions forbidding fear, taking the heaping of them as a measure of how hard that evil is to cure.

Find the tone of the code remarkable, since the discipline of war prescribed here has nothing of the harshness usual in martial law and its whole intent is to encourage the soldiers and make their service easy; set out the two grounds of confidence they were to carry, the presence of God with them and the experience they and their fathers had of his power in bringing them out of Egypt, since he who saved them from greater enemies would not let them be run down by lesser; and note that the priest who animates them is fitly the man whose office it is to pray for them.

Set the practice in its comparative frame, that almost all ancient nations took their priests to battle, since they did not expect success without the object of their adoration present and supposed they secured it by bringing his representative; and give the plain sense of the campaign directions as they stand, the priest encouraging the people with the assurance that God will go with them and fight for them.

debates.question: Which wars does this chapter govern?

sides.position: Wars against non-Canaanite nations, the Canaanite case being settled separately
Both sorts, one commanded by God and one permitted and voluntary, as Maimonides distinguishes, with different conduct required in each
War generally, not only the immediate conquest, since Moses foresees that the conquest will be gradual

debates.question: Who is the priest that addresses the army?

sides.position: Not the high priest but the priest who accompanied the army, as Phinehas did against Midian, styled by the Rabbins the anointed of the battle
A priest appointed and, the Jews say, anointed for the purpose — a fit title for the captain of our salvation
The representative of God, as almost all ancient nations took their priests to battle

outliers.note: Alone classes a law of warfare under the first commandment, arguing that religion must hold the first place even in civil government, whose direct object is only equity between men.

Alone remarks on the tone of the code itself, that the discipline of war prescribed here has nothing of the harshness usual in martial law and is designed throughout to encourage the soldiers and make their service easy.

5.pericope_label: And the officers shall speak unto the people, saying, What man is there that hath built a new house, and hath not dedicated it? let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man dedicate it. And what man is he that hath planted a vineyard, and hath not yet eaten of it? let him also go and return unto his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man eat of it. And what man is there that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her? let him go and return unto his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man take her. And the officers shall speak further unto the people, and they shall say, What man is there that is fearful and fainthearted? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren’s heart faint as well as his heart. And it shall be, when the officers have made an end of speaking unto the people, that they shall make captains of the armies to lead the people.

schools.summary: Explain the officers as the keepers of the genealogical tables, whose duty it was to appoint those bound to serve and therefore also to release such as had entered into domestic relations that would make death harder to face; give the reason for the last exemption from the Hebrew, that the brethren's heart may not flow away; and take the closing verse to mean that the same officers appointed captains over the men, rejecting the rendering that would make it a matter of leading the command, while treating those captains as leaders of the campaign whose office would cease with it.

File the exemptions under the prohibition of theft and give the reasoning: if it is hard that a man should lose by war the use of his new house or the produce of his vineyard, how much harsher to strip men of their fortunes or drive them from lands they justly call their own; and add the civil argument, that since the state needs houses built and vineyards planted, and men will not undertake such work with alacrity unless encouraged by the hope of enjoying it, God grants this indulgence.

Explain what dedicating a house meant, from the title of a psalm and from the custom of nations that consecrate part of a new house to their deity, since no pious man could think to dwell safely in a house not under divine protection; supply the marriage custom behind the third exemption, where the parties were contracted and left in their parents' houses until the bridegroom's preparations were complete; limit all these releases to a war that God allowed rather than commanded, since in the Canaanite war not even the bridegroom was exempt; and try the last exemption by the case of Gideon, where the same offer left ten thousand of thirty-two thousand standing.

debates.question: What does it mean that a man has not made his vineyard common?

sides.position: The fruit could not be eaten for three years, was devoted to the Lord in the fourth and redeemable from the priest, and was eaten in course only in the fifth
The word derives rather from piping and dancing, it being a custom to sing and dance in vineyards

debates.question: Do the exemptions apply to every war?

sides.position: Only to a war God allowed, not to one he commanded: in the Canaanite war not even the bridegroom was exempt
holders: the Jewish writers (as reported by Wesley)

sides.position: They belong to the chapter's general provision for sparing the lives of Israel's own soldiers

debates.question: What were the officers to do when they had finished speaking?

sides.position: Appoint captains over the men, the same officers who raised and organised the army
Set the captains already existing at the head of the people under their charge, since it is not likely they had captains still to make when the battle was upon them
Appoint leaders for the campaign only, whose command would cease when it was over

outliers.note: Alone reaches for Homer, whose Protesilaus went to the Trojan war leaving his wife in the deepest distress and his house unfinished, as a parallel to the hardship the exemptions were meant to prevent.

Alone turns the exemptions into an argument about property, reasoning that if it is hard to lose the use of a new house through war it is far harsher to be stripped of one’s fortune, and that the state needs men encouraged to build and plant.

10.pericope_label: When thou comest nigh unto a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace unto it. And it shall be, if it make thee answer of peace, and open unto thee, then it shall be, that all the people that is found therein shall be tributaries unto thee, and they shall serve thee. And if it will make no peace with thee, but will make war against thee, then thou shalt besiege it: And when the Lord thy God hath delivered it into thine hands, thou shalt smite every male thereof with the edge of the sword: But the women, and the little ones, and the cattle, and all that is in the city, even all the spoil thereof, shalt thou take unto thyself; and thou shalt eat the spoil of thine enemies, which the Lord thy God hath given thee. Thus shalt thou do unto all the cities which are very far off from thee, which are not of the cities of these nations.

schools.summary: Make the offer of peace a restraint on the victor, since even in lawful wars cruelty is to be repressed and bloodshed avoided as far as possible, and note that this equity was naturally implanted in all nations, which is how heralds arose; then refuse to let the harder clause pass without protest, asking how God, the Father of mercies, sanctions indiscriminate bloodshed when even heathen writers require mercy for men who lay down their arms — and answer not by defending the letter but by conceding that more was allowed the Jews for their hardness of heart than was justly lawful for them.

Set out the two outcomes of the summons plainly, a town that opens its gates becoming tributary and serving, a town that chooses war being besieged, its males put to the sword and its spoil left to the besiegers for their own maintenance; and hold the ban on the Canaanite nations to its strict terms, while confining the phrase about every breath to human beings rather than to all that lives.

Treat the summons as a rule of honour before it is a rule of war, since Israel was not to descend on a neighbour without first giving fair notice by a public statement of the ground of the quarrel — in dealing with the worst of enemies the laws of justice must be observed, and as the sword is never to be taken in hand without cause, so not without cause shown, war being an appeal in which the merits must be set forth.

Note that interpreters are greatly divided about which cities the law covers, and hold from the context that the offer of peace belongs to towns outside the seven devoted nations, whose case is settled otherwise because their idolatry was incurable and the cup of their iniquity full.

debates.question: Which cities receive the offer of peace?

sides.position: Only towns beyond the limits of the seven devoted nations, as the context shows
Cities engaged in an arbitrary war of Israel's own choosing, as distinct from the war commanded against the seven nations
Every besieged town except the Canaanite ones

debates.question: Can the killing of every male in a town that refuses terms be defended?

sides.position: It cannot be defended as it stands: even heathen writers require mercy for men who lay down their arms, and more was conceded to the Jews for their hardness of heart than was justly lawful for them
It is the stated consequence of refusing the offered peace, the women, children and cattle being spared as having had no part in holding out the siege

outliers.note: Alone challenges the justice of the law he is expounding, asking how the Father of mercies can sanction indiscriminate bloodshed when pagan moralists required mercy for the disarmed, and answering that more was conceded to the Jews than was lawful for them.

Alone gives a separate reason for each class spared — the women for the weakness of their sex, the little ones for their tender age, the cattle for their insensibility — rather than treating them as one category.

16.pericope_label: But of the cities of these people, which the Lord thy God doth give thee for an inheritance, thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth: But thou shalt utterly destroy them; namely, the Hittites, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee: That they teach you not to do after all their abominations, which they have done unto their gods; so should ye sin against the Lord your God.

schools.summary: Try to soften the sentence by translation, rendering it thou shalt utterly subdue them, so that what is decreed is the end of their political existence as a people rather than the killing of every person; support the reading from later history, since Rahab and her household were spared and the record says plainly that Solomon made the remnant of the six nations pay tribute rather than putting them to death; and restrict the word for nothing to no man, the beasts with few exceptions being given to Israel for a prey.

Keep the terms of the ban strict, so that these nations were to be altogether exterminated lest they teach Israel their abominations and sins, and read the reason clause as the ground of the sentence rather than as a qualification of it.

Explain why the Canaanites stand outside the ordinary laws of war, since God had not merely armed Israel against them but appointed the nation the minister and executioner of his vengeance, having borne with those peoples four hundred years while they grew steadily worse in their obstinacy; and add that the land itself was consecrated to God's service, so that inhabitants who could do nothing but contaminate it had to be removed.

debates.question: Does the ban require the death of every Canaanite?

sides.position: It may be rendered thou shalt utterly subdue them, so that their political existence was annihilated rather than every life taken — as the sparing of Rahab and the survival of the six nations until Solomon show
Many were suffered to live on becoming proselytes, that being one of the terms of peace
They were to be laid under the ban and altogether exterminated, that they might not teach Israel their abominations
Nothing that breatheth means no man, the beasts with few exceptions being given to Israel for a prey

outliers.note: Alone argues the ban from later history, that Rahab was spared and that the remnant of the six nations survived to be made tributary by Solomon, who therefore did not consider himself bound by this law to put them to death.

19.pericope_label: When thou shalt besiege a city a long time, in making war against it to take it, thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them: for thou mayest eat of them, and thou shalt not cut them down (for the tree of the field is man’s life) to employ them in the siege: Only the trees which thou knowest that they be not trees for meat, thou shalt destroy and cut them down; and thou shalt build bulwarks against the city that maketh war with thee, until it be subdued.

schools.summary: Attach the law about trees to the commandment against theft and draw the inference, that if God restrains the liberty of injury in the very heat of war he meant his people far more to abstain from mischief in peace; hold that though the laws of war opened the gate to plunder, the land was not to be left barren for the future, booty being taken with the advantage of the human race still in view; and give two reasons for sparing fruit-trees, that they supply food to all men and so manifest the blessing of God, and that trees are exposed and defenceless, so that war is not to be waged with them as with men.

Call the original exceedingly obscure and set four renderings side by side without choosing between them, holding that the sense is clear even where the grammar cannot be settled: the provision was merciful in sparing what yielded the fruit that supports life, and sound policy besides, since even conquerors must perish if the means of life are cut off, and it is diabolic cruelty to add the horrors of famine to the miseries of war; then narrow the prohibition to a general destruction rather than the felling of a few as the siege required, and gloss man's life as the sustenance of his life.

Render the permission closely, that only trees known not to bear edible fruit may be hewn down and a rampart built with them against the town until it come down, the verb being the one used of lofty fortifications sinking from their eminence; and trace the noun for siege to a root meaning to compress or force down, so that the same word serves both for being hemmed in and for the rampart that hems in.

debates.question: What does the clause about the tree of the field and man's life mean?

sides.position: The grammar cannot be settled and four renderings stand side by side, though the sense is plain enough: fruit-bearing trees are spared because they support life, and conquerors too must perish if the means of life are cut off
The trees are spared because they feed all men and manifest God's blessing, and because they are exposed and defenceless, so that war is not to be waged with them as with men
It means the sustenance or support of man's life

outliers.note: Alone sets out four competing renderings of the obscure clause without choosing between them, and calls it diabolic cruelty to add the horrors of famine to the miseries of war.
Alone turns the provision into an emblem, the axe laid to fruitless trees in a moral sense while trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, are never rooted up.

themes: thou shalt not destroy the trees
the tree of the field is man’s life
